content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated guidelines on the use of multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by pregnant women. These guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes, particularly in settings where micronutrient deficiencies are prevalent. Pregnant women are especially vulnerable to deficiencies in vitamins and minerals due to increased metabolic demands to support fetal growth and development. Iron deficiency is the most common micronutrient deficiency globally and is the leading cause of anemia in pregnant women. Approximately 32 million pregnant women worldwide are affected by anemia, with iron deficiency anemia accounting for 60% of cases in non-malarial areas and 50% in malaria-endemic regions. Other common deficiencies during pregnancy include folate, iodine, calcium, vitamin A, zinc, and vitamin D, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. These deficiencies are associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, such as maternal mortality, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and developmental issues in infants. The updated guideline replaces the term home fortification with point-of-use fortification to reflect the variety of settings where MNPs can be used, such as homes, schools, nurseries, and refugee camps. The guideline is intended for governments, healthcare workers, scientists, and organizations involved in designing and implementing nutrition programs and antenatal care services. It also supports efforts to achieve global health targets, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) related to ending hunger, improving nutrition, and reducing maternal and neonatal mortality. The WHO conducted a systematic review of evidence to assess the effects and safety of MNPs for point-of-use fortification during pregnancy. Two trials were included in the review, one conducted in Bangladesh and the other in Mexico, both in rural settings. These trials compared the use of MNPs with standard iron and folic acid supplementation or other micronutrient supplements. The overall quality of evidence was very low, and no significant added benefits of MNPs over standard iron and folic acid supplementation were observed in improving maternal and infant health outcomes. Based on the limited evidence available, the WHO does not recommend the routine use of MNPs as an alternative to standard iron and folic acid supplementation during pregnancy. The recommendation is classified as strong, despite the very low quality of evidence, due to the lack of demonstrated additional benefits of MNPs. The WHO will continue to monitor research developments in this area and update the guideline as new evidence becomes available. The organization welcomes suggestions for additional research questions to be evaluated in future updates.
